passage: Ulla had barely sat down at her grandmother's seventieth-birthday lunch in Tampere when Aunt Kirsi leaned over the herring. "Any special someone yet? You're twenty-one, you know." Two more relatives asked before the cake, each smiling, each warm. Ulla laughed the first time, said "Not yet" the second, and by the third she was studying the pattern on her napkin. Her cousin Abebe caught her eye and lifted the coffee pot as an excuse to stand. In the kitchen she pressed her palms on the cool counter. She knew Aunt Kirsi meant it kindly; Kirsi had married young and been happy. But every question made a wedding date feel closer, as if someone had wound a clock for her without asking.

qa.q: Where was the birthday lunch held?
qa.a: The lunch for Ulla's grandmother's seventieth birthday was in Tampere.

qa.q: How does Ulla feel by the third question, and what shows it?
qa.a: She feels pressed and uneasy. She studies her napkin, escapes to the kitchen and presses her palms on the counter, and she feels a clock has been wound for her. 🤍

qa.q: Which choice did Ulla make when the third question came, and how could she build on it?
qa.a: She stepped away to the kitchen to steady herself instead of snapping. Next she could thank Aunt Kirsi for caring, say she will share news when there is any, and turn the talk to something else, perhaps with Abebe's help.

qa.q: How might Aunt Kirsi see her own questions?
qa.a: As affection. Kirsi married young and was happy, so she probably means to wish Ulla the same joy without noticing how often the question comes.

grounding: A young adult hears relatives ask about marriage at a family gathering and feels the decision being hurried, though the concern is kind.

passage: Every tiffin hour at the design studio in Pune had turned into the same quiz. "Abhinav, twenty-two now, no? Time to look at a few biodatas," said Mr. Kulkarni from accounts, and two others nodded. Abhinav, who had joined only four months earlier, opened his mouth to say "Send me one, sir," just to end the subject. He stopped when he heard how tired the sentence sounded. Sangeeta, the senior editor, put down her spoon. "Sir, he'll tell us when there's news. Could you pass the pickle?" Later, at the water cooler, she said quietly, "They mean well. But you don't owe anyone an answer by Diwali." Abhinav nodded, surprised at how much lighter his shoulders felt.

qa.q: Who asked Abhinav about biodatas at the tiffin table?
qa.a: Mr. Kulkarni from accounts asked, and two others nodded.

qa.q: Why was Abhinav about to say "Send me one, sir"?
qa.a: He was tired of the topic and wanted the questions to stop. He felt hurried, not ready, and nearly agreed just for peace.

qa.q: Which choice kept Abhinav from a hurried yes, and what could he say himself next time?
qa.a: He stopped when he heard how tired his own sentence sounded, and Sangeeta backed him up. Next time he could politely say he will share news when there is any and change the subject.

qa.q: What might Sangeeta have been thinking when she spoke up?
qa.a: She probably saw that Abhinav was cornered and did not want him to agree just to end it, while still accepting that Mr. Kulkarni meant well.

grounding: A young adult is repeatedly asked about marriage at work and nearly agrees to a match only to stop the pressure.

passage: The engagement hall in Aminabad smelled of marigolds and frying kachoris. Asif had barely reached the buffet when Phuppo caught his sleeve. "Your cousin is settled at twenty-three. You're twenty-one now, so when is your turn?" He laughed and said something about exams. Two tables later, an uncle asked the same thing, then tapped his watch as if it were a joke. By the time the cake was cut, Asif had heard the question five times. He stepped out to the balcony, where his cousin Kashish was scrolling her phone. "Counting?" she asked. "Five," he said. "They mean well, I know. Phuppo cried at my school results." He stared at the traffic below. "But it feels like someone started a timer on me and forgot to ask if I wanted one." Kashish passed him a kachori and said nothing, which helped.

qa.q: How many times had Asif heard the question by the time the cake was cut?
qa.a: Asif had heard the question five times by the time the cake was cut.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when he said it felt like someone had started a timer on him?
qa.a: He felt pressured and a little trapped, even though he knew his relatives cared; he mentions that Phuppo cried at his school results, so the love is real, but the repeated question made him uneasy.

qa.q: What small step could help Asif at the next gathering?
qa.a: He could prepare one calm, friendly line, such as "I'll tell you when there's news," and perhaps ask a trusted relative like Kashish to change the subject when the questions pile up.

qa.q: How might Phuppo see her question differently from how Asif hears it?
qa.a: To Phuppo it is probably a caring, light question at a happy family event; she may not realise that hearing it five times in one evening makes Asif feel hurried.

grounding: It shows a young adult hearing relatives ask about marriage again and again at a gathering, feeling time pressure while knowing the concern comes from love.

passage:
"Anjali, beta, come sit. Your Mama has something to tell you."
Kishore Mama was already holding his phone out. "Very good family, Pune. The boy is an engineer. I'll send your photo tonight, no?"
"Tonight?" Anjali set down the tray of diyas. "Mama, I'm in my second year."
"Second year is the best time to start looking! These things take time."
"Then why tonight?"
Mummy laughed nervously. "He's only trying to help, Anjali."
"I know." Anjali sat down beside him. "Mama, you remembered my exam dates last year when nobody else did. So I know you care. But please don't send anything. If I ever want help, I'll ask you first. Promise."
Kishore Mama lowered the phone slowly. "First? You promise?"
"First," she said, and he put the phone in his pocket.

qa.q: Where does the family Kishore Mama mentions live?
qa.a: The family Kishore Mama mentions is in Pune.

qa.q: How can you tell that Anjali felt rushed by her uncle's offer?
qa.a: She repeats "Tonight?" and "Then why tonight?" and reminds him she is only in her second year, which shows she felt hurried and uneasy about something so big moving so fast.

qa.q: Which part of Anjali's reply helped the most, and why?
qa.a: She named his care first, by recalling that he remembered her exam dates, and then set a clear limit while promising to come to him first; that let him keep his role without rushing her. 🙂

qa.q: What is it like for Kishore Mama when Anjali asks him not to send the photo?
qa.a: He may feel a little deflated at first, since he was eager to help, but her promise to ask him first lets him feel trusted rather than rejected.

grounding: It shows a relative pressing a young adult about marriage out of real love, and how the pressure can rush a lifelong decision.

passage:
I used to mute the family chat group only during exams. Last winter I muted it for good.
It started with my cousin's wedding card. Someone replied under it, "Next is Bidisha?" with three laughing faces. Then an aunt wrote, "Don't wait too long, beta, good boys go fast." Twenty people reacted with hearts. I was in the college library, reading the same line of my notes again and again.
My cousin Mridul texted me privately a minute later: "Ignore them. Want me to post a dog photo to change the topic?" He did, and it worked for about an hour.
Looking back, nobody in that group wished me harm. My aunt sends me soup when I'm sick. But being asked in front of everyone made my life feel like a countdown I hadn't agreed to.

qa.q: What did Mridul offer to post to change the topic?
qa.a: Mridul offered to post a dog photo to change the topic.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling while reading the same line of notes again and again?
qa.a: Bidisha felt embarrassed and anxious, because the question was asked in front of the whole family group and made life feel like a countdown Bidisha had not agreed to.

qa.q: How could Bidisha answer the aunt without a fight?
qa.a: Bidisha could send the aunt a short private message, thanking her for caring and saying Bidisha will share news when there is some, so the aunt's love is honoured without adding to the pressure.

qa.q: Why might Mridul react differently from the others in the group?
qa.a: Mridul is close in age and may understand how public jokes can sting, so he offers quiet support and a distraction instead of joining the teasing.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult receiving repeated, loving but public pressure to marry, which makes the decision feel hurried.

passage:
College counsellor's note, Monday.
Damini, twenty-one, came in after the weekend at her cousin Vaibhav's wedding in Jaipur. She said she was asked about her own marriage "at least thirty times": by aunties at the mehndi, by a great-uncle during the pheras, even by the photographer. "When is your number, beta? Twenty-one is the right age. Don't wait too long." She laughed telling me, then her eyes filled. She said it felt like everyone had set a clock inside her and she could hear it ticking in class.
She was clear that her family loves her, and that her mother only wants her settled and safe. We separated the love from the timing. She wants to finish her master's first. We practised a short, warm answer: "When I'm ready, you'll be the first to know, masi." She plans to tell her mother about the master's this week, before the next wedding season. Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: How many times did Damini say she was asked about marriage?
qa.a: At least thirty times.

qa.q: How did Damini feel after the wedding weekend?
qa.a: She felt pressured and upset, laughing at first but then tearful, as if a clock had been set inside her.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Damini respond to the pressure?
qa.a: By separating the family's real love from the timing, and practising a short, warm answer she could give relatives.

qa.q: How might Damini's mother see the questions about marriage?
qa.a: Her mother probably sees them as care, wanting Damini settled and safe, without realising how much pressure they add.

grounding: It illustrates a young adult asked about marriage at every gathering who feels a clock being set, alongside real family love.
